title: Reasons of the heart
hook: Pascal: the heart has its reasons, which reason does not know

segments.voice: Yesterday, Richard Hooker. Your line was reason is a gift. Did you manage to say the other side's view back before giving yours? Day one thousand two hundred fifty-nine.

After Blaise Pascal died, the story goes, a servant found a folded paper sewn into the lining of his coat. On it Pascal had written about one night when, as he tells it, he met God. Near the top, after the date, stands a single word: fire. It names the God of Abraham, of Isaac, of Jacob, and adds: not of the philosophers and the scholars. Pascal was a mathematician, a man of proofs. And a note with no proof in it was the one he kept in his coat.

Pascal left behind a pile of notes for a book he never finished. They were gathered after his death as the Pensées, his thoughts. In one of them he writes: "The heart has its reasons, which reason does not know." The line often gets used to mean, feelings beat facts. Pascal meant something sharper. He trusted reason; he did mathematics. But he noticed that some things we know without proving them. That we're awake and not dreaming. The first principles that all our proofs start from. These, he said, we know by the heart, a kind of direct knowing underneath argument. And faith, for Pascal, lives there too. In another note he says it is the heart, not the reason, that perceives God. That isn't giving up on thinking. It's honesty about where thinking starts. Scripture gives the heart that kind of weight. Proverbs says, "Keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life." And when the shepherds have told what they saw at the manger, Luke says, "But Mary kept all these things, and pondered them in her heart." Pondering in the heart: not feeling instead of thinking, but thinking all the way down. Pascal's night of fire wasn't the end of an argument. It was more like recognizing a voice in a crowded room before you can explain how you know it. And still he went on writing arguments, because for him the head and the heart were meant to work together.

Here's the practice: trust a heart-reason. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something you know but can't fully prove. That a certain person loves you. That a choice you made was right. That a place is home. Don't argue for it. Just let it be known, the way Pascal said the heart knows. Then notice: does it hold steady when you stop defending it? If you pray, you can bring that knowing to God and rest in it. The bell holds the time.
Reasons of the heart. Pascal's line: the heart knows some things, God among them, that reason can't reach by proof alone.
Your line: the heart has reasons. Today, when you make one choice, notice whether you're listening to your heart's reasons as well as your head's. Day one thousand two hundred fifty-nine.

howItsDone: Christians read Pascal's Pensées as a classic of faith and reason; across churches, Christians speak of knowing God with the heart as well as the mind, in prayer, worship, and quiet reflection.

fork.setup: you're Pascal, a mathematician who trusts proofs. one night you meet God, and you can't prove it to anyone. what do you do with it?
options: throw it out, since it can't be proved.
write it down and keep it with you.
turn it into a mathematical proof.
fork.reveal: the story goes his note was found sewn into his coat after he died: fire, the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, not of the philosophers.

notes: Confirm the Trotter 1910 wording of Pensées 277 exactly ('The heart has its reasons, which reason does not know.').
The Memorial: 'the story goes' a servant found it sewn into his coat after his death; confirm who found it, and that 'Fire' and 'not of the philosophers and the scholars' are fairly paraphrased.
'They were gathered after his death as the Pensées' — confirm phrasing; no date given.
Examples of heart-knowledge (waking vs dreaming, first principles) paraphrase Pensées 282; confirm numbering.
French original line is from Pascal; confirm spelling and pronunciation guide.
Editor pass: corrected the placement of 'fire' in the Memorial (it comes near the top, after the date heading, not in the middle); varied the hook's closing line.

Audit: Luke 2:19 comes before the shepherds return (2:20), so 'after the shepherds leave' was a sequence error; fixed. 'when he met God' now framed as Pascal's own account, not the narrator's assertion.
